stem: During intake, collegiate sprinter Amara Okafor completes the CSAI-2 before a conference meet. Her cognitive and somatic anxiety intensity scores are well above her team's average, yet her coach notes she has run personal bests at nearly every high-stakes meet this season. Amara asks whether her nerves are a problem. Drawing on Jones's directional perspective on competitive anxiety, what additional information would most help the consultant interpret her scores?
options: How her intensity scores compare with published norms for collegiate sprinters
Whether her anxiety is mainly cognitive or mainly somatic in nature
Whether she experiences her symptoms as helpful or harmful to performance
How much her intensity scores fluctuate in the weeks between competitions
rationales: Normative comparisons describe how much anxiety she reports relative to others, which is the intensity information the consultant already has; norms cannot reveal how she reads those symptoms.
The CSAI-2 already separates cognitive from somatic anxiety, so this adds nothing new and still leaves open whether high intensity hurts her.

Jones's directional perspective holds that the same intensity of anxiety can be interpreted as facilitative or debilitative, and direction often explains performance better than intensity. Her strong results despite high intensity suggest she may read her symptoms as helpful, which only a direction rating can confirm.

Week-to-week fluctuation is a reasonable descriptive detail, but it does not address how she interprets the symptoms she has when she competes, which is the question the directional perspective raises.
takeaway: When anxiety intensity and performance don't line up, assess direction: is the athlete reading the symptoms as facilitative or debilitative?

stem: Tomasz Wierzbicki, an elite single sculler, wants to understand how his emotional state before races relates to how he performs. He says some of his best races came when he felt wound up and others when he felt calm, and he is unsure what to aim for. The consultant decides to plan the assessment around Hanin's IZOF model. Which assessment approach best fits that model?
options: Have him recall several best and worst races and rate the emotions he felt before each
Compare his pre-race anxiety scores with norms for elite rowers to find deviations
Measure his pre-race arousal and check whether it falls in the moderate range
Track only his negative emotions before races, since those are the ones that impair rowing
rationales: IZOF holds that each athlete has a personal zone of optimal emotional intensity and content, so assessment starts with the individual: retrospective ratings of emotions before best and worst performances (later checked against actual races) identify his own optimal and dysfunctional zones.
IZOF rejects group norms as the standard, because an intensity that is too high for one rower may be optimal for another.
A moderate-arousal target reflects the inverted-U hypothesis; IZOF predicts that an athlete's optimal zone can sit at low, moderate, or high intensity.
IZOF includes both pleasant and unpleasant emotions, and unpleasant ones such as tension can be part of an athlete's optimal profile, so tracking only negative emotions would miss half the picture.
takeaway: IZOF assessment is idiographic: identify the athlete's own best-performance emotional zone from his history, not from norms or a universal moderate target.

stem: The artistic director of a pre-professional ballet company asks a consultant to find out why several talented teenage dancers seem anxious and are talking about leaving. The director posts weekly casting rankings and praises dancers mainly when they outshine their peers. The consultant already plans to measure each dancer's task and ego goal orientation. Grounded in achievement goal theory, what else should the assessment capture?
options: Each dancer's trait anxiety, to identify who is most predisposed to worry about casting
Each dancer's preferred learning style for picking up new choreography
The number of hours each dancer rehearses outside company classes
How dancers perceive what the company rewards: improvement or outdoing peers
rationales: Trait anxiety is a person-level variable that may be worth knowing, but it overlooks the situational factor achievement goal theory emphasizes, and the stem points to the director's practices as a likely contributor.
Learning-style preferences are not a construct in achievement goal theory and have weak empirical support as a basis for tailoring instruction.
Rehearsal hours describe training volume, not the goal structure of the environment that achievement goal theory says shapes motivation and anxiety.

Achievement goal theory treats motivation as a product of dispositional orientation and the perceived motivational climate. Public rankings and peer-comparison praise suggest an ego-involving (performance) climate, so measuring how dancers perceive the climate is essential to interpret their anxiety and dropout talk.
takeaway: Achievement goal theory directs assessment at both the person (task/ego orientation) and the environment (perceived mastery vs. performance climate).

stem: Collegiate golfer Diego Fuentes completes the CSAI-2 before several tournaments. His results show consistently high cognitive anxiety, moderate somatic anxiety, and high self-confidence, and his scores on the course have worsened as his worry has increased. According to multidimensional anxiety theory, which finding should the consultant treat as the priority when building his plan?
options: His moderate somatic anxiety, since the theory predicts best performance with minimal bodily arousal
His high cognitive anxiety, since the theory predicts performance declines as worry increases
His high self-confidence, since the theory predicts it will mask his anxiety and reduce effort
His overall anxiety level, since the theory treats the components as one combined state
rationales: Multidimensional anxiety theory predicts an inverted-U relationship between somatic anxiety and performance, so a moderate level is close to optimal rather than a problem to eliminate.

Multidimensional anxiety theory predicts a negative linear relationship between cognitive anxiety and performance. Diego's high worry, tracking his worsening scores, is the component the theory flags as most harmful, so it should be the plan's first target.
The theory predicts a positive linear relationship between self-confidence and performance, so his high confidence is a strength to protect, not a liability.

The defining feature of multidimensional anxiety theory is that cognitive and somatic anxiety are separate components with different relationships to performance, so collapsing them loses the key information.
takeaway: Multidimensional anxiety theory: cognitive anxiety ↓ performance linearly, somatic anxiety follows an inverted-U, and self-confidence ↑ performance linearly.

stem: A consultant reviews a season of data from professional basketball player Keisha Morrow: pre-game worry ratings, warm-up heart rate, and free-throw percentage. When her worry was low, her shooting changed only gradually as heart rate rose. When her worry was high, her shooting held steady as heart rate rose and then dropped off abruptly. Which model best accounts for this pattern?
options: The inverted-U hypothesis
Drive theory
Individual zones of optimal functioning
Hardy's catastrophe model
rationales: The inverted-U hypothesis predicts a smooth, symmetrical rise and fall of performance with arousal and has no role for cognitive anxiety, so it cannot explain why the abrupt drop appears only when worry is high.

Drive theory predicts that rising arousal steadily strengthens the dominant response, a linear pattern that does not fit either the gradual curve under low worry or the sudden collapse under high worry.

IZOF describes athletes' personal optimal zones of emotional intensity, but it does not specify an interaction in which cognitive anxiety determines whether rising physiological arousal produces a gradual or a sudden change.

Hardy's catastrophe model proposes that cognitive anxiety and physiological arousal interact: with low cognitive anxiety, arousal has a mild inverted-U effect, but with high cognitive anxiety, arousal past a certain point produces a sudden, large performance drop. Keisha's data match that interaction.
takeaway: An abrupt performance collapse as arousal rises, appearing only when worry is high, is the signature of the catastrophe model.

stem: Collegiate rower Hiroshi Tanaka tells the consultant, "I keep showing up to 5 a.m. practice because I'd feel ashamed if I quit after everything my family sacrificed." He reports little enjoyment and says he isn't sure rowing matters to him anymore. Using self-determination theory to interpret this, which plan goal is most appropriate?
options: Help him explore whether rowing connects to goals and values he personally endorses
Add tangible rewards for attendance so his participation becomes more consistent
Have him recall his family's sacrifices before each practice to keep his drive high
Raise the selection pressure on the team so he works harder to keep his seat
rationales: Hiroshi describes introjected regulation: he participates to avoid guilt and shame, an internal but controlling form of motivation linked to low enjoyment. Self-determination theory recommends fostering more autonomous regulation (identified or integrated) by helping him find personally valued reasons, which also respects his freedom to decide how rowing fits his life.
Tangible rewards target external regulation and can feel controlling, moving him further from autonomous motivation rather than closer to it.
Rehearsing family sacrifices strengthens the guilt-based pressure that defines introjected regulation, which self-determination theory associates with lower well-being and enjoyment.
Heightened selection pressure adds external control; it may raise short-term effort but works against the autonomous motivation the theory links to persistence and well-being.
takeaway: Guilt- or shame-driven participation is introjected regulation; SDT-consistent plans help the athlete find personally endorsed reasons rather than add pressure or rewards.

stem: Firefighter recruit Lena Brandt must complete an aerial ladder climb to graduate from the academy. Assessment shows she has watched many classmates finish the climb and has heard steady encouragement from instructors, yet she rates her confidence as very low. She has never climbed above the third rung of the training ladder. Based on Bandura's self-efficacy theory, which plan component should take priority?
options: More videos of experienced firefighters completing the full climb smoothly
A pre-test talk from the academy captain affirming that she has what it takes
Supervised practice climbs she can complete, progressing gradually in height
Breathing training to lower her arousal on the morning of the test
rationales: Watching others succeed is vicarious experience, a weaker source than personal mastery, and she has already had plenty of it without gaining confidence.
Encouragement is verbal persuasion, generally the weakest and least durable source, and the stem shows it has not lifted her efficacy.

Bandura identifies performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) as the most powerful source of self-efficacy. A graded sequence of successful climbs gives her direct evidence that she can do the task, which observation and encouragement have not supplied.
Managing physiological states is a legitimate source of efficacy information, but calming her on test day does nothing about her lack of personal success at height, which is the main gap.
takeaway: When vicarious experience and persuasion haven't worked, build graded mastery experiences, the strongest source of self-efficacy.

stem: After losing three close matches, 15-year-old tennis player Zara Haddad tells the consultant, "I lose because I'm just not a natural like the other girls. There's no point working on my serve." Her effort in practice has dropped noticeably since. Based on attribution theory, which goal should guide the consultant's plan?
options: Help her credit losses to outside factors such as bad luck or poor officiating
Help her link losses to changeable causes she controls, such as tactics and effort
Help her accept that natural ability sets firm limits so her expectations stay realistic
Help her stop analyzing the causes of losses and focus only on stroke mechanics
rationales: Luck and officiating are external and uncontrollable; such attributions may soften disappointment but give her nothing she can act on and do not restore effort.

Zara attributes failure to an internal, stable, uncontrollable cause (lack of natural ability), the pattern Weiner's theory links to low expectations of success and reduced effort. Attribution retraining shifts explanations toward unstable, controllable causes such as tactics and effort, which sustain expectancy and motivation.
Reinforcing ability as a fixed limit strengthens the stable, uncontrollable attribution that is already undermining her motivation.
Ignoring her attributions leaves the belief driving her withdrawal intact; technical work is unlikely to stick while she believes practice is pointless.
takeaway: Attribution retraining moves failure explanations from stable, uncontrollable causes (ability) to unstable, controllable ones (effort, strategy).

stem: Elite figure skater Mei-Lin Zhou tells the consultant her confidence rises and falls with her coach's comments and with whether the judges seemed to like her last program. When asked what else makes her feel confident, she rarely mentions her training or how well she has prepared. Drawing on Vealey's work on sources of sport confidence, which planning priority is most appropriate?
options: Ask her coach to give her more frequent praise and reassurance in the days before competitions
Set her goals around earning higher component marks from the judges
Limit her contact with her coach in the weeks before major events
Build her confidence on mastery and preparation, which are largely within her control
rationales: Coach support is a recognized source of confidence, but leaning on it more keeps her confidence dependent on something outside her control and therefore fragile.
Judges' marks are an outcome she does not control, so anchoring confidence and goals to them deepens the instability she already describes.
Cutting contact removes a source of support without giving her a more stable foundation, and could strain an important working relationship.

Vealey's multidimensional view of sport confidence identifies several sources, and those rooted in mastery and physical and mental preparation are more controllable and stable than others' evaluations. Broadening her confidence to rest on these makes it less vulnerable to day-to-day feedback.
takeaway: Confidence that rests on controllable sources such as mastery and preparation is sturdier than confidence that depends on others' approval.

stem: Masters swimmer Gloria Esposito logs her anxiety daily in the week before a national championship. Her worry ratings are high and fairly steady all week, while her ratings of butterflies and muscle tension stay low until the morning of the race, peak on the blocks, and fade soon after the start. How should the consultant use this pattern in planning?
options: Start cognitive strategies early in the week, since her worry is elevated long before race day
Wait until race morning to begin any strategies, since that is when her anxiety matters
Treat the race-morning spike as a warning sign and reduce her training load that week
Plan somatic strategies for the whole week, since bodily tension is what is driving her worry ratings
rationales: Multidimensional anxiety theory describes exactly this temporal pattern: cognitive anxiety rises early and stays relatively high and stable before competition, whereas somatic anxiety stays low until shortly before the event, peaks at the start, and dissipates once performance begins. Her plan should address worry well before race day and save somatic techniques for the pre-start window.
Waiting until race morning ignores a week of elevated worry, the component the theory links most directly to poorer performance.
A somatic spike right before the start is the normal pattern the theory predicts, not a sign of overtraining, and training load is a coaching decision outside the consultant's role.
Her bodily tension is low for most of the week, so week-long somatic strategies mismatch her data; the theory treats the two components as distinct rather than one driving the other.
takeaway: Cognitive anxiety builds early and stays high; somatic anxiety spikes near the start and fades once performance begins, so time interventions accordingly.

stem: Judoka Rafael Moreira, a national team member, recalls his best and worst matches. Before his best matches he felt tense, slightly irritated, and determined; before his worst he felt relaxed, content, and a little sluggish. He asks whether he should work on getting rid of the irritation. Consistent with the IZOF model, how should the consultant interpret this profile when planning?
options: As evidence that his best results came in spite of harmful emotions he should reduce
As a sign that he should aim for the calm, content state most athletes prefer
As his personal optimal profile, including unpleasant emotions that help him compete
As unreliable, since recalled emotions cannot be used to set performance targets
rationales: IZOF rejects the assumption that unpleasant emotions are always harmful; his data show irritation and tension consistently accompany his best matches.
IZOF is idiographic, so what most athletes prefer is not a target, and for Rafael the relaxed, content state is linked to his worst matches.

Hanin's IZOF model holds that each athlete has an individual optimal emotional profile that can include unpleasant emotions that are functional for that athlete. His plan should help him reliably reach his own zone, not strip out emotions that help him.
Recall of emotions before best and worst performances is a core IZOF method for identifying individual zones, ideally confirmed with ratings before upcoming matches.
takeaway: In IZOF, unpleasant emotions such as tension or irritation can be part of an athlete's optimal zone; don't assume they must be eliminated.

stem: Professional basketball point guard Imani Brooks is excellent at reading the defense and planning plays, but her coach notes that she keeps weighing options even after deciding to shoot, and her percentage on open shots has dropped. Using Nideffer's model of attention, which attentional shift should her plan target at the moment of the shot?
options: From broad-external to broad-internal, to plan the next play
From broad-internal to narrow-external, to lock onto the target
From narrow-external to broad-external, to track all teammates
From narrow-internal to broad-internal, to review the play call
rationales: Shifting into broad-internal focus would deepen the analyzing she already does too much of at the moment of execution.

Nideffer's model places attention on width and direction dimensions. Weighing options is broad-internal (analysis and planning), while executing a shot calls for a narrow-external focus on the target, so her plan should train a clean shift from analysis to the rim once she decides to shoot.
Broad-external focus suits reading the defense before the decision, not executing the shot; widening attention at release adds irrelevant cues.
Reviewing the play call is broad-internal analysis, which is the habit interfering with her execution.
takeaway: Nideffer: assess (broad-external), analyze (broad-internal), rehearse (narrow-internal), execute (narrow-external); performance suffers when an athlete is stuck in the wrong quadrant.

stem: A consultant working with a youth wrestling club reviews TEOSQ results and coach interviews for four wrestlers. Time for individual sessions is limited, so the consultant must decide whose motivation needs attention first. According to achievement goal theory, which wrestler's profile suggests the greatest risk of withdrawing effort and dropping out?
options: Malik: high task orientation, low ego orientation, moderate perceived ability
Ravi: high task and high ego orientation, high perceived ability
Sven: high ego orientation, low task orientation, high perceived ability
Tobi: high ego orientation, low task orientation, low perceived ability
rationales: A strong task orientation defines success as personal improvement, which achievement goal theory links to sustained effort regardless of perceived ability.
High task orientation alongside high ego orientation tends to protect motivation, because success can still be found in improvement when comparisons go badly.
An ego-oriented wrestler who believes he is capable usually stays engaged while he keeps winning; he is vulnerable later, but his profile is not the most at risk now.

Nicholls's achievement goal theory predicts that a strong ego orientation combined with low perceived ability is the most maladaptive profile: when success means beating others and the athlete doubts he can, avoiding challenge, reduced effort, and dropout become likely.
takeaway: High ego orientation plus low perceived ability is the achievement goal profile most at risk of effort withdrawal and dropout.

stem: A consultant administers the Group Environment Questionnaire to a collegiate volleyball team that has struggled with in-game coordination. Players score high on both social cohesion scales but low on group integration–task, and several say the team gets along well off the court but isn't pulling in the same direction during matches. Which planning priority best fits these results?
options: Add more off-court social events to strengthen the bonds players already share
Conclude that cohesion is not a concern, since the social cohesion scores are high
Target task cohesion by clarifying roles and building shared team goals
Meet individually with the lowest-scoring players to raise their task commitment
rationales: Social cohesion is already high, so more social events target a strength and leave the task-cohesion gap untouched.
Carron's model treats task and social cohesion as distinct; high social scores do not offset low task cohesion, which is the dimension most tied to coordinated performance.

The GEQ separates task from social cohesion, and low group integration–task means players do not see the team as united around its goals. Team building aimed at shared goals, clear roles, and agreed standards addresses that dimension directly.
Low group integration–task describes how players see the team as a whole, so singling out individuals misreads a group-level result and risks scapegoating.
takeaway: Read GEQ results by dimension: high social cohesion with low task cohesion calls for task-focused team building (goals, roles, standards).

stem: A police academy asks a consultant to design a resilience program. Interviews show that many cadets view demanding training scenarios as threats they hope to avoid, and academy leaders are considering removing the most stressful scenarios. Based on Fletcher and Sarkar's grounded theory of psychological resilience, which program aim is most appropriate?
options: Build protective psychological factors and train cadets to appraise hard scenarios as challenges
Remove the most stressful scenarios until cadets report feeling ready to face them
Screen applicants for resilience, since it is a fixed trait that training cannot change
Train cadets only to lower their heart rates during scenarios, since arousal drives poor responses
rationales: Fletcher and Sarkar found that psychological factors such as positive personality, motivation, confidence, focus, and perceived social support protect performers from the potential negative effects of stressors, partly by promoting challenge appraisals and helpful meta-cognitions. Building these factors while cadets face demanding scenarios fits the model.

Their model describes resilience as developing through engagement with stressors; removing the demands takes away the experiences in which resilience is built and does not prepare cadets for real duty.
The grounded theory frames resilience as a process shaped by modifiable psychological factors, not a fixed trait to screen for.
Arousal control can be one useful tool, but the model locates resilience mainly in psychological factors and how stressors are appraised, so a physiology-only program misses the core mechanism.
takeaway: Resilience develops through engagement with stressors, supported by psychological factors that promote challenge appraisals, not by removing all adversity.

stem: Six weeks after an esports organization assembles a new five-player roster, the polite early scrims have given way to open arguments over shot-calling and who plays which role. The alarmed general manager asks whether the roster should be rebuilt. Using Tuckman's model of group development, how should the consultant interpret this situation and plan?
options: As a failed roster that should be restructured quickly before the conflict spreads further
As the expected storming stage, with sessions planned to clarify roles and set norms
As the performing stage, with the consultant stepping back so the team self-manages
As the adjourning stage, with planning for an orderly transition of players out
rationales: Conflict after an initial polite phase is a normal developmental step, so treating it as proof of failure would be premature and would restart group formation.

Tuckman's model describes forming (polite orientation), then storming (conflict over roles, influence, and direction), then norming and performing. Arguments over roles six weeks in fit storming, and helping the team clarify roles and agree on norms supports the move to norming.
Performing involves smooth, interdependent work toward shared goals, which this roster has not yet reached.
Adjourning refers to a group disbanding after its task is complete; nothing suggests this roster is ending.
takeaway: Conflict over roles after a polite start is Tuckman's storming stage; facilitate role clarity and norms rather than dismantling the group.

stem: Two paramedics, Oluwaseun and Bridget, work the same shifts with the same call volume. Bridget describes busy nights as tough but manageable, citing her training and a supportive partner. Oluwaseun describes them as overwhelming and says he never knows whether he can handle the next call. Using Lazarus's transactional model of stress, which explanation should guide the consultant's plan for Oluwaseun?
options: His stress mainly reflects a stable personality trait that intervention is unlikely to change
His stress reflects a lack of motivation for the job, which should be the plan's focus
His stress reflects the objective intensity of the calls, which should be the main target
His stress reflects appraising the demands as exceeding his resources for coping
rationales: The transactional model emphasizes changeable appraisals and coping rather than fixed traits, so this explanation would leave little for the plan to work on.
Nothing in the stem suggests low motivation; his distress centers on doubting he can cope, not on a lack of interest in the work.
Both paramedics face the same objective demands, yet only one experiences them as overwhelming, which shows the demands alone do not explain his stress.

Lazarus's transactional model holds that stress arises from appraisal: primary appraisal of what is at stake and secondary appraisal of whether one's coping resources are adequate. Oluwaseun's doubt about handling the next call points to a threat appraisal driven by perceived low resources, so the plan should target his coping resources and how he appraises demands.
takeaway: In the transactional model, stress depends on the appraised balance of demands and coping resources, not on the demands alone.

stem: Conservatory pianist Anaya Deshpande is preparing for a high-pressure audition and asks the consultant to help her refine an imagery script. Her current script describes the hall, the piano, and the audience in vivid visual detail but says nothing about her own physical or emotional reactions. According to Lang's bioinformational theory, which revision would most strengthen the script?
options: Add response details, such as her quickened heartbeat and her fingers pressing the keys
Add more visual detail about the hall's lighting, seating, stage layout, and audience members
Shorten the script so it covers only the moment she walks onto the stage
Switch to an external camera view so that she watches herself perform
rationales: Lang's bioinformational theory proposes that images contain stimulus propositions (features of the scene) and response propositions (the performer's physiological, behavioral, and emotional reactions), and that imagery has more impact when response propositions are included. Her script has only stimulus content, so adding her own responses is the key revision.
More scene description adds still more stimulus propositions, the element the script already has in abundance.
Shortening the script to one moment removes rehearsal of the performance itself and does not add the response content the theory emphasizes.
Imagery perspective is a separate design choice; changing it does not supply response propositions, and an external view can make her bodily reactions less vivid.
takeaway: Bioinformational theory: imagery scripts work better when they include response propositions (what the performer feels and does), not just scene details.

stem: Survey and observation data from a youth gymnastics club show that gymnasts feel capable and connected to their teammates, but they report having no say in practice and rarely hearing why drills matter. Coaches give commands without explanation. Grounded in self-determination theory, which element should be central to the consultant's plan?
options: A points-and-prizes system that publicly rewards gymnasts for visible effort in each practice
More frequent technical corrections from coaches during each session
Coach training in giving reasons for activities and offering choices within limits
Additional team-bonding activities to deepen connections among gymnasts
rationales: Tangible rewards for effort can feel controlling and do not address the unmet need the data reveal, which is autonomy.
More corrections target competence, a need the gymnasts already report as satisfied, and frequent directives could further reduce their sense of choice.

Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic needs. Here autonomy is the unmet one, and autonomy-supportive coaching, such as giving rationales, offering choices within limits, and acknowledging athletes' perspectives, directly addresses it.
Relatedness is already a strength for these gymnasts, so bonding activities would not address the autonomy gap.
takeaway: Match the intervention to the unmet SDT need; when autonomy is thwarted, train coaches in rationale-giving and choice within structure.

stem: A community aquatics program asks a consultant to help a group of 9- to 11-year-olds who are afraid to jump into the deep end. The children are not yet ready to attempt the jump themselves, but the instructor can show them one short demonstration, live or on video, first. Based on self-efficacy theory, which demonstration would most likely raise the children's efficacy?
options: A video of a national-level diver performing a flawless entry from a high board
The instructor jumping in while telling the children how easy it is
An older teen swimmer who jumps in immediately and without any hesitation
A child their age who looks hesitant at first but then jumps in successfully
rationales: An elite diver is very dissimilar to the children in age and skill, so the demonstration offers little evidence that they can do it too.
An adult instructor is a dissimilar model, and saying the task is easy adds only verbal persuasion, a weaker source of efficacy.
An older, confident swimmer is more similar than an elite diver but still differs in age and ability, and a model who shows no fear gives fearful children less to identify with.

Bandura's theory holds that vicarious experience raises efficacy most when observers see a model similar to themselves succeed. A same-age peer who shows initial hesitation and then copes successfully is a similar coping model, which is especially persuasive for fearful learners.
takeaway: Vicarious experience works best with similar models; a peer coping model is especially useful for fearful learners.

stem: Two distance runners, Kofi and Anders, each narrowly miss qualifying for a national final. Kofi tells the consultant, "I skipped too many tempo runs this block." Anders says, "I just don't have the build for this event." According to Weiner's attribution theory, which prediction should most influence the consultant's planning?
options: Kofi is likelier to lose hope, since he blamed himself for the missed time
Anders is likelier to expect future failure, as his cause is stable and uncontrollable
Both are equally at risk, since both made internal attributions for the disappointing result
Neither is at risk, since both took personal ownership of the result
rationales: Kofi's attribution is internal but unstable and controllable; Weiner's theory links that pattern to guilt and renewed effort, not hopelessness.

In Weiner's theory, the stability dimension drives expectations of future success, and controllability shapes emotions and effort. Anders's attribution to body build is stable and uncontrollable, predicting low expectancy and reduced motivation, so his explanation is the bigger planning concern.
Locus of causality is only one dimension; the runners differ on stability and controllability, which lead to very different predictions.
Internal attributions are not automatically adaptive; an internal, stable, uncontrollable cause such as innate build is the pattern most associated with helplessness.
takeaway: Stability predicts future expectancy and controllability predicts emotion and effort; internal-stable-uncontrollable attributions for failure are the most damaging.

stem: Collegiate diver Callum Reid and a teammate report similarly high pre-meet anxiety intensity. The teammate says a racing heart helps her feel sharp, while Callum says the same symptoms mean he is about to fall apart, and his scores suffer. Consistent with the directional perspective on competitive anxiety, which plan goal fits Callum best?
options: Help him interpret his symptoms as signs of readiness rather than signs of threat
Lower his symptom intensity until it falls below his teammate's reported level
Teach him to avoid noticing his bodily sensations in the minutes before each dive
Reassure him that anxiety intensity has no real effect on diving performance
rationales: The directional perspective holds that performers can interpret the same anxiety intensity as facilitative or debilitative, and Hanton and Jones showed that cognitive skills can help athletes come to view their symptoms as facilitative. Since the teammate thrives at the same intensity, Callum's debilitative interpretation is the most useful target.
His teammate's level is an arbitrary benchmark, and the stem shows that the same intensity can accompany good performance, so intensity alone is not the core problem.
Trying not to notice bodily sensations is an avoidance strategy that tends to backfire and leaves his threat interpretation unchanged.
Anxiety can affect performance, so blanket reassurance is inaccurate and ignores his debilitative interpretation.
takeaway: When two performers share the same anxiety intensity but different outcomes, target the debilitative interpretation, not just the intensity.

stem: During a debrief after a training exercise, members of a police tactical team give conflicting accounts of who was responsible for clearing which room and which hand signal meant hold. Each officer performs well individually, but the team's entry was slow and uncoordinated. Which concept best explains the breakdown and should guide the consultant's plan?
options: Low social cohesion, so the plan should emphasize off-duty team bonding
Social loafing, so the plan should make each officer's individual effort more identifiable
Weak shared mental models, so the plan should align roles, cues, and sequences
Over-arousal, so the plan should add breathing drills before each entry
rationales: Nothing suggests the officers dislike one another; the problem is inconsistent understanding of the task, which bonding activities would not fix.
Social loafing is reduced effort in a group, but these officers are trying hard; they are simply working from different assumptions.

Shared mental models are team members' overlapping knowledge of roles, cues, and procedures that lets them anticipate one another and coordinate. Conflicting beliefs about responsibilities and signals indicate weak shared mental models, so pre-briefs, rehearsal, and structured debriefs that align that knowledge are the right focus.
Arousal could play some role in a high-stakes entry, but disagreement about who does what and what signals mean is a knowledge problem, not an arousal problem.
takeaway: Good individuals who coordinate poorly often lack shared mental models; build common knowledge of roles, cues, and sequences.

stem: Professional tennis player Sofia Lindqvist, who had worried all week about her ranking, suddenly lost five straight games after leading comfortably. At the changeover she took a few breaths and felt slightly calmer, but her play did not recover. Reviewing the match with her afterward, which guidance best reflects the catastrophe model?
options: Slightly lowering her arousal should restore her play, since the drop mirrors the rise
Raising her intensity further after a collapse is the quickest way to regain her edge
Recovery requires lowering arousal well below the collapse point and resetting her worry
The collapse shows that any physiological arousal harms her performance and must be eliminated
rationales: The catastrophe model predicts hysteresis: once performance collapses under high cognitive anxiety, a small reduction in arousal does not retrace the path back up, which is consistent with her changeover experience.
With cognitive anxiety high, more physiological arousal pushes her further past the catastrophe threshold, so psyching up would worsen the problem.

Hardy's catastrophe model holds that under high cognitive anxiety, rising arousal can trigger a sudden drop, and because of hysteresis recovery is not a simple reversal. She needs to bring arousal well below the level at which she collapsed and address her worry before rebuilding toward her optimal state, so her routine should prepare her to do that.
The model does not say arousal is always harmful; with low cognitive anxiety, physiological arousal can support performance, so eliminating it misreads the theory.
takeaway: After a catastrophe-style collapse, small calming steps won't restore play (hysteresis); substantial arousal reduction plus cognitive reset comes first.

stem: A consultant runs weekly mental skills sessions with a collegiate soccer team. So far the consultant has lectured, assigned mandatory worksheets, and reminded players that the coach will check completion. Attendance is steady, but players seem disengaged and few report using the skills on the field. Which adjustment is most consistent with self-determination theory?
options: Invite players to choose which skills to work on and explain how each links to their goals
Have the coach announce playing-time consequences for players with incomplete worksheets
Offer gift cards each week to the players who complete the most worksheets on time and in full
Add a graded quiz at the end of each session so that players stay accountable
rationales: Self-determination theory predicts that controlling delivery yields compliance without internalization. Offering meaningful choice and a clear rationale supports autonomy, which promotes more self-determined engagement and greater use of the skills outside sessions.
Threatening playing time adds external pressure that may increase worksheet completion but further undermines autonomous motivation to use the skills.
Contingent tangible rewards are often experienced as controlling and can reduce interest in the activity itself, shifting motivation toward external regulation.
Graded quizzes add evaluative pressure and treat the sessions as an obligation, the opposite of the autonomy support the theory recommends.
takeaway: Compliance without engagement signals a controlling climate; SDT points to choice and rationale, not more pressure or rewards.

stem: During scenario-based training, police recruits face a simulated armed suspect. In the highest-stress version, recruit Dana Kowalczyk locks onto the suspect's weapon and fails to notice a second person entering from the side, a cue she catches easily in calmer versions. Which explanation, based on cue utilization theory, should guide the consultant's adjustment to her training?
options: Her arousal was too low, leaving her attention broad, unfocused, and easily distracted
She lacks scanning skill, so scanning must be retaught from the beginning
Her attentional capacity is fixed, so she is unsuited to high-stress roles
High arousal narrowed her attention until relevant peripheral cues dropped out
rationales: The miss happens only in the highest-stress version, which points to arousal that is too high, not too low.
She detects the second person easily in calmer versions, so the skill exists; the problem appears only under heightened arousal.
Cue utilization theory describes attention as changing with arousal, not as a fixed capacity, and her good performance in calmer versions argues against this conclusion.

Easterbrook's cue utilization theory holds that rising arousal narrows attention, first screening out irrelevant cues and then, at high levels, relevant ones. Losing a peripheral threat only under peak stress fits that pattern, so training should build arousal regulation and practice scanning under gradually increasing stress.
takeaway: Missing relevant cues only under peak stress signals arousal-driven attentional narrowing; train arousal control and scanning under graded stress.

stem: A consultant observes a youth basketball coach who posts a ranked list of players' free-throw percentages, directs most praise to the top shooters, and groups players by ability for drills. Several lower-ranked players have stopped trying hard in practice. In coaching the coach, which change is most consistent with creating a task-involving motivational climate?
options: Keep the ranked list but add a weekly prize for the three most accurate shooters
Recognize each player's personal improvement and effort instead of public rankings
Move the lower-ranked players to a separate group so they feel less pressure
Praise only game results so that players learn what really counts in competition
rationales: Prizes for the top shooters intensify normative comparison, the hallmark of an ego-involving climate that is already discouraging lower-ranked players.

Achievement goal theory distinguishes task-involving (mastery) climates, which define success as personal improvement and effort, from ego-involving climates built on comparison. Shifting recognition to self-referenced progress and effort is the core of mastery-climate coach training and supports continued effort from all players.
Ability grouping is itself a feature of ego-involving climates, and a separate low group can signal low ability and further reduce effort.
Praising only results reinforces an outcome- and comparison-based definition of success, strengthening the ego-involving climate.
takeaway: A task-involving climate recognizes individual improvement and effort; public rankings, ability grouping, and results-only praise create ego-involving climates.

stem: Renée Dubois, 52, joined a supervised exercise program six weeks ago after medical clearance. She tells the consultant she is thinking of quitting because heavy breathing and sore legs during sessions prove her body just can't do this anymore, even though she has completed every workout. Based on self-efficacy theory, which adjustment should the consultant make?
options: Encourage her to train harder so that soreness comes to feel like a badge of toughness
Ask the instructor to tell her more often during sessions that she is doing well
Show her videos of very fit adults exercising comfortably at high intensities
Help her reinterpret breathlessness and soreness as normal responses to training
rationales: Pushing harder raises the very sensations she is misreading and risks discouraging her further without changing how she interprets them.
Verbal persuasion is a weaker source of efficacy and is unlikely to outweigh the bodily evidence she believes she is getting in every session.
Very fit models are dissimilar to her, so their ease offers little vicarious evidence about what she can do and may highlight the gap.

Bandura lists physiological and emotional states as a source of efficacy information; what matters is how people interpret them. Renée reads normal exertion as incapacity, so reframing those signals, alongside highlighting that she has completed every workout, addresses the source lowering her efficacy.
takeaway: Bodily sensations influence efficacy through their interpretation; reframe normal exertion signals rather than adding persuasion or harder training.

stem: A fitness center asks a consultant to help instructors improve attendance in a 10-week group exercise class for adults. Members rarely talk to one another, and many stop coming by the fourth week. Drawing on Carron and Spink's team-building approach for exercise groups, which strategy should the consultant coach the instructors to deliver?
options: Give each member a private program they can complete alone on their own schedule
Give the class a group identity, shared norms, and regular partner interaction
Post each member's attendance rank publicly to spark friendly competition
Raise workout intensity so members see their fitness gains more quickly
rationales: Moving members to solo programs removes the group context that team building relies on to strengthen cohesion and adherence.

Carron and Spink's team-building protocol for exercise classes targets cohesion through group distinctiveness (such as a class name), group norms, and interaction and communication among members. Greater cohesion in exercise groups is associated with better attendance and lower dropout.
Public attendance rankings introduce normative comparison and may embarrass members who are struggling, which works against a cohesive class.
Higher intensity can increase discomfort and dropout among newer exercisers and does not address the low interaction that the stem identifies.
takeaway: In exercise groups, team building that creates distinctiveness, norms, and member interaction builds cohesion, which supports adherence.

stem: Before a championship game, a consultant leads a collegiate field hockey team through a group relaxation script. Afterward, forward Nia Achterberg says she feels flat. Her performance history shows she plays best when she feels highly energized and a bit on edge. Consistent with the IZOF model, what adjustment should the consultant make for Nia?
options: Give her energizing strategies to raise her intensity into her own optimal zone
Continue the relaxation script, since lower arousal benefits all athletes before games
Teach her to stop monitoring her feelings so she doesn't overthink before games
Match her intensity to the team average so the whole group prepares in one state
rationales: IZOF holds that optimal emotional intensity is individual and can be high. Nia's history places her zone at high intensity, so after relaxation drops her below it, she needs energizing strategies to move back into her zone.
Assuming lower arousal helps everyone contradicts IZOF; for Nia, relaxation has moved her away from the state linked to her best play.
Self-monitoring is how she recognizes whether she is in her zone, so suppressing it removes the information IZOF-based preparation depends on.
A team average ignores individual differences in optimal intensity, the central claim of IZOF.
takeaway: Group preparation should allow individual adjustment; an athlete with a high-intensity optimal zone may need energizing, not relaxation.

stem: A company's virtual wellness challenge awarded points and gift cards for logging walks. Employees who enjoyed walking before the challenge now say walking feels like a chore, and once the rewards ended their activity fell below what it had been beforehand. As the consultant helps redesign the program, which explanation and adjustment best fit self-determination theory?
options: The rewards were too small, so the next challenge should offer larger prizes
Employees lack walking skills, so the program should add technique coaching
Interest naturally fades over time, so future challenges should be shorter
The rewards felt controlling, so emphasize choice and personal reasons to walk
rationales: Larger contingent rewards would likely intensify the controlling effect that the data suggest undermined interest.
Nothing indicates a skill deficit; the change is in how employees experience walking, not in their ability to walk.
A drop below baseline after rewards end, among people who previously enjoyed the activity, is better explained by the rewards themselves than by a natural fading of interest.

Cognitive evaluation theory, part of self-determination theory, predicts that expected tangible rewards experienced as controlling can undermine intrinsic motivation, leaving people less engaged once rewards stop. Redesigning around autonomy, with choice and personally meaningful reasons, supports more self-determined activity.
takeaway: Expected, controlling rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation (cognitive evaluation theory); design for autonomy instead.

stem: Late in a lopsided game, collegiate center fielder Mateo Ruiz finds himself noticing crowd chatter, the scoreboard, and teammates' banter, and he is slow to react when a fly ball heads his way. In close games he is sharp and quick off the mark. Based on cue utilization theory, which adjustment should the consultant help him use in low-stakes moments?
options: Calming breaths between pitches to lower his arousal even further
A brief activation routine to raise arousal and narrow attention to the batter
Deliberately widening his attention so that he takes in more of the whole ballpark
Mentally reviewing his swing mechanics so his mind stays engaged in the field
rationales: His arousal is already low in blowouts; lowering it further would keep attention broad and prolong the problem.

Cue utilization theory holds that at low arousal attention is broad and takes in irrelevant cues, while a moderate rise narrows attention so irrelevant cues drop out. A brief activation routine before each pitch raises arousal toward his optimal level and refocuses him on relevant cues such as the batter and the ball.
His attention is already too broad, which is why irrelevant cues are crowding in; widening it further adds more distraction.
Thinking about hitting while in the field is an internal focus on an irrelevant task and would slow his reaction to the ball even more.
takeaway: Cue utilization works both ways: too little arousal leaves attention too broad, so a modest activation boost can screen out irrelevant cues.

stem: After a narrow loss, players on a professional rugby team spend the debrief blaming the referee and the weather. The head coach asks the consultant to help run the next debrief. Based on attribution theory, which adjustment is most likely to support players' motivation going forward?
options: Guide players to identify causes they can control, such as defensive structure and effort
Agree that the referee and the weather decided the match, to protect players' confidence
Emphasize that the opponent simply has more naturally gifted players than they do
Skip any discussion of causes and move straight to planning the next fitness block
rationales: Weiner's attribution theory links controllable and unstable attributions for failure to sustained expectancy and effort. Steering the debrief toward factors the team controls and can change, such as structure, decisions, and effort, gives players something to act on.
External, uncontrollable explanations can protect self-esteem briefly, but they leave players with nothing to change and can lower persistence.
Attributing the loss to the opponent's innate talent is stable and uncontrollable, the pattern most linked to lowered expectations and effort.
Avoiding causes leaves the unhelpful attributions in place and misses the debrief's chance to guide how players explain the loss.
takeaway: In debriefs, guide attributions for losses toward controllable, changeable causes to sustain expectancy and effort.

stem: Pole vaulter Ingrid Solberg has failed at a new height in her last eight practice attempts. Before each attempt, the consultant has told her, "You've got this," but she says the encouragement now makes her feel worse. Based on Bandura's account of the sources of self-efficacy, which adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Make the encouragement more emphatic and offer it before every attempt
Have her watch video of elite vaulters clearing heights well above hers
Work with her coach to set heights she can clear, then progress in small steps
Stop practicing at the new height until her confidence returns on its own
rationales: Verbal persuasion is a weak source of efficacy, and its credibility drops when it contradicts repeated failure, so more of it is likely to deepen her discouragement.
Elite vaulters are dissimilar models, so watching them offers little evidence about what she can do and may widen the perceived gap.

Bandura identifies mastery experiences as the strongest source of self-efficacy, and persuasion that conflicts with direct experience loses credibility. Collaborating with her coach on achievable heights that progress gradually rebuilds efficacy from successful performances, while respecting the coach's role in training decisions.
Avoidance provides no new efficacy information, so confidence has nothing to rebuild from, and avoiding the height may strengthen her doubts.
takeaway: When encouragement clashes with repeated failure, switch to engineered mastery experiences; persuasion can't outweigh direct evidence.

stem: Startup founder Priscila Navarro has an investor pitch in two weeks. She tells the consultant, "I know how big this meeting is, and I'm fine presenting the product, but if they ask about our financials I won't know what to say." Using Lazarus's model of stress appraisal, which focus for the next session best targets her secondary appraisal?
options: Persuade her that the pitch matters far less than she believes it does
Teach a relaxation technique for her to use only if she panics in the room
Explore memories of difficult public speaking experiences from her childhood
Review her preparation and resources for handling the toughest investor questions
rationales: Changing how much the meeting matters targets primary appraisal (what is at stake), not her judgment about whether she can cope, and minimizing a genuinely important meeting is unlikely to be credible.
A relaxation technique held in reserve for panic manages the stress response after the fact; it does not change her evaluation of whether she has what she needs to handle the questions.
Exploring childhood history drifts from performance-focused work toward a therapeutic focus and does not address her current, specific coping concern.

In Lazarus's model, secondary appraisal is the evaluation of one's coping resources and options. Her worry centers on not being able to answer financial questions, so reviewing and strengthening her preparation and resources for that challenge targets secondary appraisal directly.
takeaway: Primary appraisal asks what is at stake; secondary appraisal asks whether I can cope, so strengthen resources to change it.

stem: During tournament matches, esports player Jae-won Park dwells on a mistake from earlier rounds and misses information on the minimap about enemy movement. In practice debriefs, he can describe exactly what he should have noticed. Using Nideffer's model of attention, which refocusing cue should the consultant help him build into his in-game routine?
options: A cue to shift from narrow-internal focus to narrow-external focus on his aim
A cue to shift from broad-external focus to broad-internal planning of strategy
A cue to shift from internal rumination to broad-external awareness of the game
A cue to stay narrow-internal until he has fully corrected the earlier mistake
rationales: A narrow-external focus on aim suits the moment of execution but would still miss the wide-ranging information about enemy movement he needs.
Shifting into broad-internal planning keeps his attention inside his head, which is where it is already stuck.

Nideffer's model describes attention on width and direction dimensions. Dwelling on past mistakes is an internal focus, while tracking enemy movement across the map requires broad-external attention, so a cue that ends rumination and returns him to broad-external scanning matches the demands of the moment.
Staying in an internal focus during play prolongs the rumination that is causing him to miss critical external information; analysis belongs in the debrief.
takeaway: When an athlete is stuck internally and missing environmental information, a refocusing cue should shift attention to broad-external.

stem: Coaches at a youth soccer academy, worried about players' well-being, have dropped competitive selection matches, stopped giving critical feedback, and step in whenever a drill becomes frustrating. Players now struggle badly when they face setbacks at tournaments. Drawing on resilience research in sport, which adjustment should the consultant recommend to the coaches?
options: Reintroduce graded challenges and honest feedback while keeping strong support in place
Withdraw from tournaments as well until the players feel ready to handle setbacks
Restore heavy pressure and harsh criticism so the players toughen up as quickly as possible
Accept that resilience is largely innate and focus on recruiting tougher players
rationales: Resilience research in sport, including Fletcher and Sarkar's work, indicates that resilience develops when performers engage with manageable stressors while feeling supported. Reintroducing appropriate challenge and honest feedback within a supportive environment gives players chances to build coping resources.
Removing still more challenge extends the overprotection that left players unprepared, and it delays rather than builds their capacity to cope.
High challenge without support tends to overwhelm young athletes and can harm well-being; resilience research pairs challenge with support rather than replacing one with the other.
Resilience is described as a dynamic process shaped by psychological factors and the environment, not a fixed trait, so recruiting for it ignores what coaches can develop.
takeaway: Resilience grows from manageable challenge paired with support; removing all adversity or removing all support both undermine it.

stem: During the off-season, a consultant holds weekly video calls with a group of para swimmers who train remotely in different cities. The calls focus on reviewing each swimmer's training metrics. The swimmers say they feel capable and like choosing their own sessions, but they feel isolated and less motivated. Which adjustment is most consistent with self-determination theory?
options: Add more detailed metrics so each swimmer can track progress more closely
Let each swimmer take on even more responsibility for designing training
Replace the group calls with individual emailed progress reports
Build in time for the swimmers to share experiences and support one another
rationales: Detailed metrics feed competence, a need the swimmers already report as met, and keep the calls focused on numbers rather than connection.
The swimmers already feel autonomous in their training, so more independence does not address the need that is going unmet.
Individual reports would reduce contact even further and deepen the isolation that is lowering motivation.

Self-determination theory identifies relatedness, feeling connected to and cared for by others, as a basic need alongside autonomy and competence. These swimmers report satisfied autonomy and competence but low relatedness, so peer connection is the adjustment that targets the unmet need.
takeaway: Diagnose which SDT need is unmet; for isolated remote athletes, build connection rather than more data or independence.

stem: Three weeks before a world championship, a minor illness cost alpine skier Lukas Brenner a week of training. In a session he says his confidence has disappeared because the work isn't there anymore. Drawing on Vealey's sport-confidence research, which approach should the consultant take in this session?
options: Tell him that confidence is a fixed trait he will rediscover once racing begins
Review his training history and results to reconnect him with evidence of his preparation
Encourage him to focus on how much his rivals may also have struggled with setbacks this season
Suggest he lower his goal to simply finishing the race without a crash
rationales: Vealey's model treats sport confidence as having state as well as trait components, and state confidence can be rebuilt; waiting for racing to restore it leaves him unsupported at a critical time.

Vealey's research identifies physical and mental preparation and mastery as key sources of sport confidence. Lukas is discounting a season of preparation because of one missed week, so reviewing concrete evidence of his training and accomplishments rebuilds confidence from sources he controls.
Rivals' struggles are an uncontrollable, situational source, so confidence built on them is fragile and turns attention away from his own preparation.
Lowering his goal sidesteps the confidence problem and may signal that the consultant also doubts his preparation.
takeaway: Rebuild shaken sport confidence from controllable sources, especially evidence of preparation and mastery.

stem: Midway through a training block, junior track cyclist Ayesha Rahman's coach keeps telling her to just do her best in each session, and her effort varies widely from day to day. The consultant is helping the coach refine the goal-setting process. According to Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory, which adjustment is most likely to improve her effort and persistence?
options: Keep the do-your-best approach but add more encouragement during sessions
Set specific, challenging session targets and give feedback on her progress
Set easy targets she will always reach so that she never feels discouraged
Focus her solely on the season's outcome goal of winning the national title
rationales: Locke and Latham found that do-your-best instructions give no clear standard, so effort tends to vary; encouragement does not supply the missing standard.

Goal-setting theory holds that specific, difficult goals with feedback outperform vague do-your-best goals because they direct attention, mobilize effort, increase persistence, and prompt strategy development. Concrete session targets with progress feedback address her inconsistent effort directly.
The theory links goal difficulty to effort: easy goals demand little and so mobilize little, whereas harder goals, given commitment and ability, produce more effort and persistence.
A distant outcome goal alone does little to guide effort in day-to-day sessions and depends on factors she does not control; it works best when paired with specific performance and process targets.
takeaway: Specific, challenging goals with feedback beat do-your-best goals by directing attention, effort, persistence, and strategy.

stem: A consultant has been teaching progressive muscle relaxation to amateur triathlete Bao Nguyen, whose CSAI-2 and interview data show high cognitive anxiety and low somatic anxiety. After three weeks of practice, Bao says his body feels relaxed but he still cannot stop worrying about the race. Which adjustment best reflects the matching principle for anxiety interventions?
options: Shift toward cognitive strategies such as restructuring worries and refocusing attention
Lengthen each muscle relaxation session until his worry finally begins to decrease
Add a pre-race psych-up routine to raise his physiological activation level
Add heart-rate biofeedback to reduce his bodily arousal even further before races
rationales: Multidimensional anxiety theory separates cognitive and somatic anxiety, and the matching hypothesis proposes that interventions work best when they target the type of anxiety a person experiences. Bao's problem is worry, so cognitive strategies fit better than more somatic relaxation.
Muscle relaxation has already lowered his bodily tension without touching his worry, so more of the same technique mismatches his cognitive anxiety.
His somatic anxiety is already low and his difficulty is worry, so raising physiological activation addresses neither the type nor the direction of his problem.
Biofeedback that lowers bodily arousal is another somatic technique aimed at the component that is already low.
takeaway: Match the technique to the anxiety: cognitive strategies for worry, somatic techniques for bodily tension.

stem: Players on a professional ice hockey team each report confidence in their own skills, but in interviews several say the team always falls apart on the penalty kill. Their penalty-kill success rate has dropped across the season. Based on Bandura's concept of collective efficacy, which adjustment should the consultant and coaching staff make to practices?
options: Have each player set individual skill goals for their own penalty-kill duties
Build penalty-kill drills the unit can succeed at together, then raise the difficulty
Show the players video of the league's best penalty-killing teams in action
Have the captain give a speech affirming the team's toughness and resolve before each game
rationales: Individual goals target personal efficacy, which is already high; the doubt is about how the unit performs together.

Collective efficacy is a group's shared belief in its combined capability to perform a task. Like individual self-efficacy, it is built most powerfully through mastery experiences, so graded drills in which the penalty-kill unit succeeds together give the group direct evidence of its joint capability.
Watching elite teams is a vicarious source and is generally weaker than the group's own success, especially when the models are not similar to the team.
A captain's speech is verbal persuasion, a weaker source that is unlikely to outweigh repeated breakdowns on the penalty kill.
takeaway: Confident individuals can still doubt the team; build collective efficacy through shared, graded mastery experiences.

stem: A regional theatre company's cast has worked closely together for a five-month production run that ends next week. Several actors say they feel unsettled and unsure how to say goodbye, and the director asks the consultant to help during the final days. Using the expanded version of Tuckman's model of group development, which approach best fits this stage?
options: Run role-clarification exercises to settle lingering conflicts about responsibilities
Introduce new group norms to raise performance standards for the final shows
Facilitate a closing session to reflect on contributions and prepare for transition
Encourage the cast to avoid discussing the ending so that they stay focused
rationales: Role-clarification work fits the storming stage; the cast's concern now is the group's ending, not conflict over roles.
Setting norms fits the norming stage; at the end of a long run, the group's task is to close well rather than renegotiate standards.

The adjourning stage, added in a later revision of Tuckman's model, describes a group disbanding after completing its task, often with mixed feelings. A structured closing that acknowledges contributions and helps members prepare for what comes next addresses that stage directly.
Avoiding the topic leaves the actors' unsettled feelings unaddressed and may distract them more than an open, planned closure would.
takeaway: When a group is ending (adjourning), facilitate closure: reflect on contributions and prepare members for transition.
